title: Understanding the Beat-to-Beat Variations of P-Waves Morphologies in AF Patients During Sinus Rhythm: A Scoping Review of the Atrial Simulation Studies

subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Framework for Scoping Reviews in Atrial Simulation Research
subsections.content: The methodological framework for scoping reviews in atrial simulation research draws primarily on the foundational work of Arksey and O’Malley, who established a five-stage process including identifying the research question, searching for relevant studies, selecting studies, charting data, and collating, summarizing, and reporting results ref [1]. This framework has since been refined by Peters et al., who introduced the term 'systematic scoping review' to emphasize rigor in search strategy, study selection, and data extraction, particularly valuable in heterogeneous domains such as computational atrial electrophysiology ref [2]. Further clarification of terminology and methodological transparency was advocated by Colquhoun et al., who recommended standardized definitions and reporting practices to enhance reproducibility and comparability across studies ref [3]. In the context of atrial simulation, these guidelines enable researchers to systematically map the evolving landscape of computational models used to analyze P-wave morphology variability, distinguishing between structural, electrophysiological, and autonomic modulators of atrial activation. The inclusion of consultation exercises with clinicians and modelers, as suggested by Arksey and O’Malley, further enhances the relevance of findings to clinical translation. Given the interdisciplinary nature of atrial simulation research—spanning cardiology, biomedical engineering, and computational biology—adherence to a structured scoping framework ensures comprehensive coverage while avoiding the pitfalls of ad hoc literature synthesis.

subsections.subsection_title: P-Wave Morphology as a Noninvasive Marker of Atrial Substrate and AF Risk
subsections.content:
P-wave morphology has emerged as a sensitive noninvasive marker of the underlying atrial substrate and risk for atrial fibrillation (AF), reflecting regional variations in conduction, fibrosis, and anatomical remodeling that are not always captured by P-wave duration alone. Unlike prolonged P-wave duration, which primarily indicates global conduction delay, morphological variability captures localized conduction disturbances, altered activation sequences, and heterogeneous atrial depolarization patterns, making it particularly valuable in patients with paroxysmal AF and no structural heart disease ref [5]. Beat-to-beat analysis of P-wave morphology has demonstrated that dynamic changes in shape, amplitude, and axis during sinus rhythm correlate with the presence of atrial substrate predisposing to AF initiation ref [7]. Studies have shown that increased P-wave morphological variability (PMV) is associated with both the prediction of impending paroxysmal AF episodes and the likelihood of recurrence after catheter ablation, with PMV ≥20% independently predicting successful circumferential pulmonary vein isolation ref [4], ref [8]. Novel indices such as the Cross-Correlation Index, Amplitude Dispersion Index, and Warping Index quantify this variability with high sensitivity and specificity, outperforming traditional metrics in distinguishing AF patients from controls ref [6]. These findings underscore that P-wave morphology is not merely a passive reflection of atrial size but an active indicator of electrophysiological instability and structural remodeling.

The clinical utility of P-wave morphology extends beyond diagnosis to risk stratification and therapeutic monitoring, offering a low-cost, widely accessible tool for identifying patients at high risk of AF progression or recurrence. Integration of morphological variability into automated ECG analysis platforms holds promise for real-time, beat-to-beat assessment of atrial substrate integrity, enabling personalized preventive strategies.

subsections.subsection_title: Atrial Electrophysiological Substrates for P-Wave Morphology Variability
subsections.content:
Beat-to-beat variability in P-wave morphology during sinus rhythm in atrial fibrillation (AF) patients is fundamentally influenced by heterogeneous electrophysiological substrates across the atria. Regional differences in action potential duration (APD), refractoriness, and ionic current densities—particularly in the left atrium (LA) versus right atrium (RA)—create spatial gradients in excitation propagation that manifest as P-wave morphological fluctuations. Computational studies demonstrate that shorter AP refractoriness in the LA promotes faster reentrant rotation, dominating atrial activation patterns and altering the timing and direction of wavefronts that generate the P-wave ref [11]. Heterogeneity in ionic channel expression, such as variations in transient outward potassium current (I_to) and inward rectifier potassium current (I_K1), further contributes to regional AP morphology differences, directly impacting P-wave shape and duration ref [16]. These ionic disparities are exacerbated in pathological states, including familial AF linked to gain-of-function mutations in KCNQ1 (I_Ks) or KCNJ2 (I_K1), which abbreviate APD and ERP, thereby increasing tissue susceptibility to conduction heterogeneity and P-wave instability ref [9], ref [10], ref [11].

Chronic pharmacological remodeling, such as that induced by β-blocker therapy, modifies these substrates by downregulating I_to and I_K1, prolonging APD and ERP, and reducing spatial dispersion of repolarization—effects that may attenuate P-wave variability ref [13]. Canine and human atrial models incorporating anatomical and electrophysiological heterogeneity confirm that conduction slowing and block at boundaries between regions with differing refractoriness generate complex activation sequences, which are reflected in dynamic P-wave morphologies ref [12], ref [14]. Thus, P-wave morphology variability during sinus rhythm serves as a noninvasive biomarker of underlying atrial substrate heterogeneity, reflecting the interplay of ionic channel expression, structural organization, and remodeling processes that predispose to AF initiation and maintenance.

subsections.subsection_title: Computational Modeling of Atrial Structure and Activation for P-Wave Analysis
subsections.content:
Computational modeling of atrial structure and activation has become indispensable for deciphering the electrophysiological origins of P-wave morphology variability in atrial fibrillation (AF) patients during sinus rhythm. High-resolution, image-based models derived from MRI and CT scans now enable the integration of detailed anatomical features—including the crista terminalis, pectinate muscles, Bachman’s bundle, and pulmonary vein sleeves—into simulations that accurately reproduce activation sequences and P-wave patterns ref [20]. These models incorporate three-dimensional myofiber anisotropy and regional wall thickness variations, which critically influence conduction velocity and wavefront curvature, thereby shaping P-wave morphology ref [19]. The incorporation of patient-specific fibrosis distributions, modeled through conduction heterogeneities or myocyte-fibroblast coupling, has further refined the ability to predict localized conduction delays and P-wave fragmentation ref [24]. Recent advances in personalization frameworks have enabled calibration of conduction velocity and tissue conductivity to match clinically recorded P-wave durations and activation maps, enhancing predictive fidelity ref [23]. Validation against intracardiac electrograms and optical mapping data has confirmed that simulated wave directions and activation times closely align with empirical measurements, supporting the use of these models as noninvasive surrogates for atrial substrate characterization ref [9].

Moreover, the integration of ex vivo human atrial structural data—including transmural fibrosis gradients and 3D fiber orientation—has revealed distinct structural 'fingerprints' associated with P-wave abnormalities, linking specific fibrosis patterns and wall thickness profiles to altered activation dynamics ref [13]. Patient-derived models have demonstrated that reentrant drivers in AF are spatially constrained to regions with high fibrosis density and entropy, which also correspond to regions of P-wave distortion during sinus rhythm ref [12]. The development of multiscale sheep atrial models, incorporating biophysically realistic cell electrophysiology and anatomical fidelity, has further enabled the dissection of how structural heterogeneity modulates P-wave variability across species ref [21]. Together, these computational approaches provide a mechanistic bridge between atrial substrate remodeling and noninvasive ECG biomarkers, positioning atrial simulation as a cornerstone for personalized AF risk stratification.

subsections.subsection_title: Autonomic and Structural Modulators of Atrial Dynamics in AF
subsections.content:
Autonomic nervous system modulation plays a critical role in shaping atrial electrophysiological dynamics that predispose to atrial fibrillation (AF), even during sinus rhythm. Heterogeneous sympathetic denervation, as demonstrated in canine models, creates spatially discordant effective refractory periods and increases dispersion of repolarization, thereby establishing a substrate for sustained AF ref [25]. This denervation-induced heterogeneity is not mirrored by parasympathetic changes, as shown by preserved parasympathetic nerve labeling despite sympathetic defects, highlighting the selective impact of sympathetic remodeling ref [25]. Conversely, cholinergic activation via acetylcholine induces rapid, organized reentry by stabilizing primary spiral wave generators and exacerbating refractoriness heterogeneity, challenging the classical multiple-wavelet hypothesis and implicating vagal tone in AF initiation and maintenance ref [6].

Structural modulators, particularly atrial dilatation, further interact with autonomic influences to promote conduction abnormalities. Computational modeling reveals that acute atrial stretch induces mechanoelectric feedback, leading to conduction slowing and block—key precursors to reentry—through altered gap junction coupling and membrane properties ref [14]. These structural changes, often present in early AF, amplify the arrhythmogenic potential of autonomic imbalances by creating anatomical and functional barriers to uniform activation. Together, autonomic remodeling and structural distortion form a synergistic substrate that modulates P-wave morphology variability during sinus rhythm, reflecting underlying atrial substrate instability prior to overt arrhythmia recurrence.

subsections.subsection_title: Simulation-Based Validation of P-Wave Changes Post-Ablation and Therapeutic Interventions
subsections.content:
Computational models have been instrumental in validating the electrophysiological changes in P-wave morphology following atrial ablation and pharmacological interventions, providing mechanistic insights beyond clinical electrocardiographic observations. Simulation studies have demonstrated that localized ablation near rotor cores can terminate atrial fibrillation (AF) and restore sinus rhythm, with concomitant normalization of P-wave morphology due to reduced atrial heterogeneity and reentry suppression ref [28]. In silico investigations of I_Kur inhibitors reveal that their antiarrhythmic efficacy is highly dependent on kinetic properties, with prolonged refractoriness reducing rotor stability and promoting P-wave stabilization post-treatment ref [29]. Furthermore, state-dependent blockade of I_Kur in chronic AF models shows that despite channel downregulation, residual I_Kur remains a critical determinant of action potential duration and P-wave dynamics, influencing therapeutic outcomes ref [30]. Combined blockade of I_Kur and I_Na has been shown to synergistically suppress reentry and enhance P-wave regularity in atrial tissue simulations, suggesting a promising multi-channel strategy ref [10].

The accuracy of P-wave reconstruction post-intervention is critically influenced by the spatial resolution of mapping and ablation targeting. In silico studies indicate that electrogram density must exceed 0.4 mm to reliably detect rotor tips whose ablation correlates with P-wave normalization, while lower resolutions risk mislocalization and suboptimal therapeutic outcomes ref [16]. Dynamic approximate entropy (DApEn) mapping, validated in computational models, enables precise identification of rotor locations whose ablation leads to consistent P-wave morphological recovery ref [17]. Novel ablation strategies, including targeted circular and linear lesions near phase singularity sites, have been shown in bilayer atrial models to terminate rotors more effectively than conventional pulmonary vein isolation, resulting in more predictable P-wave restoration ref [17]. These findings underscore the necessity of high-fidelity computational validation to optimize ablation protocols and pharmacological regimens aimed at restoring sinus rhythm and normalizing P-wave characteristics.

subsections.subsection_title: P-Wave Morphology as a Marker of Atrial Electrophysiology in Sinus Rhythm
subsections.content: P-wave morphology serves as a noninvasive biomarker of atrial electrophysiology during sinus rhythm, reflecting the spatiotemporal dynamics of atrial depolarization. Its shape is determined by the origin of sinus activation, the pattern of interatrial conduction, and the anatomical configuration of the atria, making it sensitive to subtle conduction abnormalities not captured by P-wave duration alone ref [5]. Computational studies using the equivalent double layer source model have demonstrated that precise simulation of atrial activation sequences can reproduce clinically observed P-wave morphologies, validating the link between intracardiac electrical propagation and surface ECG patterns ref [35]. The site of earliest right atrial activation and its proximity to key interatrial conduction pathways—such as Bachmann’s bundle and posterior interatrial connections—significantly influence P-wave terminal force in lead V₁, with anterior or inferior activation sites yielding markedly different morphologies ref [36]. Furthermore, the elimination of pulmonary vein myocardial sleeves following ablation alters P-wave duration and terminal morphology, indicating that ectopic atrial activation sources can modulate sinus rhythm signatures even in the absence of overt structural disease ref [5]. These findings underscore that P-wave morphology encodes integrated information on atrial conduction heterogeneity, fibrosis distribution, and functional remodeling, offering a window into subclinical electrophysiological changes preceding arrhythmia recurrence.

subsections.subsection_title: Role of Pulmonary Veins and Sinoatrial Node Pathways in P-Wave Generation and AF Initiation
subsections.content:
The sinoatrial node (SAN) and its exit pathways (SEPs) play a critical role in orchestrating the initial atrial activation that defines P-wave morphology during sinus rhythm. Computational models have demonstrated that the spatial distribution and conduction properties of SEPs significantly influence the direction and timing of atrial depolarization, thereby shaping the P-wave’s axis and duration ref [37]. Disruptions in SAN exit dynamics—whether due to structural remodeling or ion channel dysfunction—can lead to aberrant activation patterns, potentially predisposing to ectopic triggers and arrhythmogenesis ref [13].

Concurrently, the pulmonary veins (PVs) serve as a major source of ectopic activity capable of initiating atrial fibrillation (AF), particularly through pacemaking cardiomyocytes embedded in their myocardial sleeves. Biophysically detailed models of human PV cells reveal distinct ionic profiles between pacemaking and non-pacemaking subtypes, with enhanced I_NCX, I_Ca-L, and I_Ca-T currents enabling automaticity that can override SAN dominance ref [38]. These ectopic foci, when coupled with anatomical heterogeneity, can trigger reentry or focal firing that disrupts normal sinus rhythm ref [39].

Computational simulations further indicate that PV size and coupling impedance critically determine whether focal activity evolves into sustained reentry, with longer PVs (>2 cm) showing significantly higher reentry prevalence ref [14]. The interplay between SAN exit integrity and PV arrhythmogenicity underscores a dual-pathway model of AF initiation, where SAN dysfunction may permit PV dominance, while PV-triggered ectopy can destabilize normal atrial activation, altering P-wave morphology even during sinus rhythm ref [17].

subsections.subsection_title: Atrial Structural and Electrical Remodeling in AF and Its Impact on Sinus Rhythm Dynamics
subsections.content:
Atrial structural and electrical remodeling in atrial fibrillation (AF) profoundly alters the electrophysiological substrate even during sinus rhythm (SR), contributing to persistent P-wave morphological variability. Fibrotic infiltration, visualized via late gadolinium enhancement MRI, disrupts normal conduction patterns and introduces spatial heterogeneity in activation, which simulations show can persistently distort P-wave morphology despite restoration of SR, as demonstrated in patient-specific models ref [43]. Concurrently, chronic AF induces significant electrical remodeling, including downregulation of L-type calcium current (I_CaL), ultrarapid potassium current (I_Kur), and transient outward current (I_to), alongside upregulation of inward rectifier potassium current (I_K1) and sodium-calcium exchanger (I_NCX), leading to action potential shortening and loss of rate adaptation ref [46]. These ionic changes, validated in human atrial computational models, result in altered repolarization dynamics that manifest as prolonged early repolarization phases and flattened plateaus in P-waves, even in the absence of ongoing arrhythmia ref [45]. Furthermore, three-dimensional virtual atrial models reveal that non-uniform APD shortening, particularly at junctions such as the crista terminalis and pulmonary vein ostia, creates localized conduction delays and re-entry vulnerabilities that persist in SR, thereby sustaining P-wave instability ref [5].

The interplay between structural fibrosis and ion channel remodeling generates a self-sustaining substrate where even transient SR episodes exhibit abnormal activation sequences, explaining why P-wave morphology remains altered post-ablation or cardioversion. Computational studies confirm that fibrosis distribution, not merely its extent, dictates the spatial pattern of P-wave distortion, while ionic remodeling modulates the temporal dynamics of atrial depolarization ref [43]. This dual remodeling mechanism underscores why P-wave analysis in SR may serve as a non-invasive biomarker of residual atrial substrate abnormality after AF ablation.

subsections.subsection_title: Computational Modeling of Atrial Activation and P-Wave Generation
subsections.content:
Computational modeling of atrial activation and P-wave generation has advanced significantly through the integration of high-resolution anatomical data and biophysically detailed electrophysiological models. Image-based models derived from magnetic resonance and serial microscopy data have enabled the reconstruction of realistic 3D atrial geometries, including specialized conduction pathways such as the crista terminalis, Bachman’s bundle, and pulmonary vein sleeves, which critically influence the spatiotemporal pattern of atrial depolarization ref [48]. These models, when coupled with anisotropic fiber orientation and heterogeneous ionic properties, accurately simulate the sequence of atrial activation and its corresponding ECG signature, particularly the P-wave morphology ref [18]. The dipole-current source approach has further refined P-wave prediction by decomposing left and right atrial contributions, demonstrating that interatrial conduction delays and regional refractoriness directly modulate P-wave shape during sinus rhythm ref [47]. Personalized models incorporating patient-specific anatomy and conduction velocity heterogeneities have improved the correlation between simulated and recorded P-wave durations, enabling clinical translation ref [50]. Moreover, simulations using human atrial models derived from MR images have validated the role of structural complexity in generating P-wave variability, particularly near the pulmonary veins and interatrial septum ref [13]. These frameworks collectively provide a mechanistic basis for interpreting beat-to-beat P-wave morphological changes as reflections of underlying atrial substrate dynamics.

Recent advances have also integrated virtual cohorts to account for inter-individual variability, enhancing the robustness of P-wave predictions across populations ref [50]. The inclusion of detailed sinoatrial node exit pathways and pulmonary vein electrophysiology has further elucidated how ectopic activity and conduction delays initiate abnormal activation patterns that manifest as P-wave alterations even in sinus rhythm ref [16]. Such models are now instrumental in distinguishing between benign morphological variations and those indicative of arrhythmogenic remodeling, offering a quantitative platform for pre-ablation planning and post-intervention assessment.

subsections.subsection_title: Limitations in Personalizing Atrial Models for P-Wave Prediction
subsections.content:
Personalizing atrial models for accurate P-wave prediction remains challenged by incomplete anatomical and electrophysiological characterization of the sinoatrial node (SAN) and its exit pathways. While recent advances have revealed the SAN's extended anatomical distribution and heterogeneous ion channel expression, most computational models still oversimplify its geometry and pacemaking dynamics, leading to inaccuracies in simulating beat-to-beat P-wave morphology variations ref [5]. Furthermore, the spatial resolution of clinical imaging modalities often fails to capture microstructural details such as fibrosis patterns, myofiber orientation, and interstitial conductivity gradients, which critically influence atrial activation sequences and ECG signatures ref [47]. Even when high-resolution MRI or CT data are available, the transformation of anatomical structures into biophysically accurate tissue models introduces significant uncertainty due to assumptions in tissue conductivity, cell membrane kinetics, and coupling between atrial regions ref [52].

The dipole-current source approach, while effective for decomposing left and right atrial contributions to the P wave, relies on idealized source distributions that may not reflect the true complexity of SAN-driven activation ref [52]. Additionally, inter-patient variability in autonomic tone, ion channel expression, and atrial remodeling—particularly in AF patients transitioning to sinus rhythm—is rarely incorporated into personalized models, limiting their predictive power. The absence of patient-specific SAN exit pathway mapping further impedes accurate simulation of the earliest activation sites, a key determinant of P-wave morphology. These limitations underscore the gap between theoretical modeling capabilities and clinical data availability, hindering the translation of in silico P-wave predictions into reliable diagnostic tools.

subsections.subsection_title: Mechanisms of Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Morphology Variability in Sinus Rhythm
subsections.content:
Beat-to-beat variability in P-wave morphology during sinus rhythm arises from dynamic changes in the site of earliest right atrial activation (EAS) and the conduction pathways through interatrial connections. Computational studies demonstrate that minor shifts in EAS location—such as from mid-septal to anterior-superior or inferior regions—can alter the direction and timing of atrial depolarization, leading to significant changes in P-wave amplitude and terminal force in lead V₁, with deviations up to 2.0-fold between adjacent sites. The integrity and dominance of interatrial conduction routes, particularly Bachmann’s bundle versus posterior interatrial connections, further modulate left atrial activation patterns and contribute to morphological variability. When posterior interatrial connections are non-conductive, P-wave terminal force increases by up to 150% in inferior EAS scenarios, highlighting the compensatory role of alternative conduction pathways.

Beyond anatomical determinants, beat-to-beat fluctuations may also reflect transient autonomic modulation, subtle changes in atrial refractoriness, or microstructural heterogeneity affecting conduction velocity. These factors, though not always captured in static anatomical models, are critical for interpreting the inherent variability observed in clinical ECG recordings. The interplay between EAS dynamics and interatrial conduction architecture thus provides a mechanistic framework for understanding why P-wave morphology remains inherently variable even in the absence of structural disease or arrhythmia, underscoring its potential as a sensitive biomarker of atrial substrate instability.

subsections.subsection_title: Role of Atrial Simulation Models in Interpreting P-Wave Dynamics
subsections.content:
Atrial simulation models play a pivotal role in deciphering the mechanistic underpinnings of beat-to-beat P-wave morphology variability during sinus rhythm in atrial fibrillation (AF) patients. By integrating patient-specific anatomical data with biophysically detailed electrophysiological properties, these models enable the non-invasive interrogation of atrial activation sequences that underlie P-wave dynamics, which are often obscured in clinical ECG recordings. Computational frameworks have demonstrated that subtle variations in sinoatrial node exit pathways, interatrial conduction delays, and regional conduction heterogeneity can manifest as distinct P-wave morphologies, even in the absence of overt arrhythmia ref [55]. Furthermore, virtual human atria models have been instrumental in linking ectopic foci and localized conduction abnormalities to P-wave alterations, providing a theoretical basis for interpreting multi-lead ECG patterns ref [5]. These simulations allow for controlled manipulation of ion channel expression, fibrosis distribution, and tissue anisotropy—factors that are difficult to isolate experimentally—thereby revealing how structural and electrical remodeling contribute to P-wave variability ref [53].

The integration of high-resolution imaging with computational electrophysiology has further enhanced the predictive capacity of these models, enabling the generation of synthetic ECGs that closely match clinical recordings. This synergy not only validates model accuracy but also facilitates the identification of novel biomarkers for AF predisposition. As such, atrial simulation models serve as a critical bridge between macroscopic ECG observations and microscopic cellular mechanisms, offering a platform for hypothesis testing and personalized risk stratification in pre-arrhythmic states.

subsections.subsection_title: Multiscale Modeling of Atrial Tissue for P-Wave Dynamics
subsections.content:
Multiscale modeling of atrial tissue has emerged as a critical approach to elucidate the origins of beat-to-beat P-wave morphology variations during sinus rhythm in atrial fibrillation (AF) patients. By integrating high-resolution anatomical data from magnetic resonance imaging with biophysically detailed ionic models, researchers have reconstructed patient-specific atrial geometries that capture the structural heterogeneity influencing electrical propagation. Virag et al. demonstrated that a 3D atrial model derived from segmented MRI data can reproduce complex arrhythmogenic patterns, providing a foundation for linking tissue architecture to P-wave dynamics ref [49]. Further advances have incorporated anisotropic myocardial architecture and microstructural variability, revealing how localized fibrotic remodeling and gap junctional uncoupling generate spatially heterogeneous conduction patterns that manifest as P-wave variability ref [6]. These models bridge cellular electrophysiology with whole-organ ECG signatures, enabling the simulation of P-wave morphology changes arising from subcellular ion channel behavior to macroscopic wavefront propagation.

To capture the stochastic nature of atrial activation, cellular automaton models have been employed to simulate large-scale electrical dynamics with reduced computational cost, allowing long-term analysis of P-wave fluctuations under varying structural conditions ref [57]. Such approaches reveal that minor differences in myocardial architecture—such as strand orientation, branching density, or fibrosis distribution—can significantly alter the spatiotemporal sequence of atrial activation, thereby modulating P-wave shape and duration. The integration of these multiscale frameworks with clinical ECG data has begun to establish predictive relationships between structural 'fingerprints' and individualized P-wave signatures, paving the way for personalized risk stratification in AF progression.

subsections.subsection_title: Impact of Atrial Remodeling on P-Wave Variability
subsections.content:
Atrial remodeling, particularly in the context of persistent atrial fibrillation, significantly alters electrophysiological properties that manifest as beat-to-beat P-wave morphology variability during sinus rhythm. Computational studies have demonstrated that electrical remodeling—characterized by downregulation of potassium currents, altered calcium handling, and shortened action potential duration—induces spatial heterogeneity in repolarization, which directly impacts the timing and amplitude of atrial depolarization waves. Ref [1] showed that incorporating AF-induced remodeling into a heterogeneous human atrial model drastically shortened simulated Ta-waves and increased repolarization dispersion, suggesting analogous effects on P-wave dynamics due to shared underlying ionic mechanisms. Furthermore, structural remodeling, including T-tubule loss and fibrotic infiltration, disrupts transverse conduction and promotes localized conduction delays, contributing to P-wave fragmentation and variability. Ref [3] introduced a human atrial myocyte model with variable T-tubule organization, revealing that T-tubule disorganization promotes calcium mishandling and spatially heterogeneous excitation, which may underlie beat-to-beat P-wave instability even in sinus rhythm. These findings highlight that both electrical and structural remodeling act synergistically to amplify P-wave variability, potentially serving as a biomarker for subclinical arrhythmogenic substrate.

Recent in-silico studies further support that patient-specific remodeling patterns, including regional fibrosis distribution and ion channel expression gradients, lead to distinct P-wave signatures that correlate with clinical outcomes. The integration of these remodeling features into multiscale models enables the prediction of P-wave morphology changes prior to overt arrhythmia recurrence, offering a mechanistic basis for personalized risk stratification.

subsections.subsection_title: Computational Models of Atrial Myocyte Electrophysiology in Sinus Rhythm
subsections.content:
Computational models of human atrial myocyte electrophysiology in sinus rhythm have been pivotal in elucidating the ionic determinants of action potential morphology and rate adaptation. Early models, such as the Nygren et al. formulation, established a foundational framework by integrating key K⁺ currents—including the sustained outward current (Iₛᵤₛ) and transient outward current (Iₜₒ)—to replicate human atrial action potential profiles under physiological pacing conditions ref [62]. Subsequent refinements by Courtemanche et al. incorporated detailed formulations of L-type Ca²⁺ current, Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger, and background currents, demonstrating that rate-dependent action potential shortening arises from incomplete recovery of Iₖₗ and deactivation of delayed rectifier currents ref [12]. More recent models have emphasized the role of sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Ca²⁺ dynamics, showing that peripheral SR release sites critically modulate action potential duration by coupling Ca²⁺ transients to sarcolemmal currents, while central release sites govern fire-diffuse-fire propagation ref [60]. The work by Maleckar et al. further advanced model accuracy by reparameterizing Iₜₒ and Iₖᵤᵣ to enforce charge conservation and reproduce experimentally observed rate dependence ref [61]. These models collectively reveal that atrial myocyte behavior in sinus rhythm is governed by a delicate interplay between K⁺ conductances, Ca²⁺ handling, and Na⁺ homeostasis, with perturbations in any component altering repolarization kinetics and predisposing to arrhythmia.

The integration of atrial-specific ionic densities, such as reduced Iₖ₁ and elevated Iₖᵤᵣ, into comprehensive models has enabled accurate simulation of resting membrane potential and repolarization reserve in human atria ref [45]. These models have also clarified how variations in Iₜₒ density account for inter-individual P-wave morphology heterogeneity, even in sinus rhythm, by altering the spatial and temporal profile of atrial activation. Furthermore, simulations incorporating dynamic intracellular Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ concentrations have revealed that Na⁺ accumulation during tachycardia indirectly modulates AP duration via NCX and Na⁺/K⁺ pump activity, providing a mechanistic basis for rate-adaptation beyond channel kinetics alone ref [60], ref [45]. Collectively, these computational advances have transformed atrial myocyte models from descriptive tools into predictive platforms for understanding the electrophysiological substrate underlying beat-to-beat P-wave variability.
